title: Heads of Security: Learned Attention Gates Improve Prompt Injection Robustness
summary: We introduce Heads of Security (HoS), a prompt injection defense that enforces instruction-data separation via a small set of learned per-head attention gates. HoS learns how each head should redistribute attention between trusted and untrusted tokens, enabling models to reason over untrusted content without following injected instructions. We evaluate HoS on Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct and GPT-OSS-20B. We compare it against SecAlign++, a state-of-the-art finetuning-based defense, and ASIDE, a defense that, like ours, builds instruction-data separation into the model architecture. We show that HoS offers greater robustness to adaptive attacks, better performance on standard utility benchmarks, and matches top performance on standard agentic prompt injection benchmarks. More specifically, the black-box RL-Hammer attack reaches 97% ASR against GPT-OSS-20B and 85% against SecAlign, but only 10% against HoS. Claudini, a state-of-the-art white-box attack, strengthened against HoS through autoresearch, requires 3 times more FLOPs to reach the same ASR on HoS as it does on GPT-OSS-20B or SecAlign. HoS preserves base-model utility across standard multiple-choice benchmarks and prompting setups, whereas SecAlign and ASIDE degrade in few-shot settings. On agentic benchmarks with static attacks, HoS and SecAlign perform similarly and substantially improve the security-utility trade-off over the base model. ASIDE struggles with tool use, achieving only 10% utility. These results show that prompt injection robustness can be achieved and improved through targeted attention interventions.

title: Scaling Laws for Tool-Use Agents via Controllable Environment Synthesis
summary: We explore how to build performant large language model (LLM) tool-use agents that complete complex, multi-step tasks. Specifically, we study how data composition in synthetically generated tool-use environments affects the training of such agents. To do so, we propose the SynthAPI pipeline, which explicitly controls the diversity of generated environments along the axes of tools, tasks, and the databases on which the tools operate. By systematically varying SynthAPI's generation controls in 458,752 tasks across 849 trained models of four different sizes, we derive a scaling law that predicts downstream tool-use agent generalization based on the scale and composition of the synthesized environments. These predictable relationships reveal several lessons for scaling tool-use agent data. As data budgets grow, scaling tool and database diversity becomes more effective than increasing the number of tasks, and increasing data complexity yields larger gains. Scaling according to these findings yields agents that outperform models trained on data from prior work in large-scale tool-use agent and synthetic environment generation across four evaluation benchmarks.

title: Timestral
summary: We introduce Timestral, a family of four time series foundation models for probabilistic forecasting, with 5M, 28M, 123M, and 209M parameters. Timestral sets a new state of the art on GIFT-Eval, TIME, and fev-bench, where Timestral-209M and Timestral-123M take the top two places on every metric. We achieve this with three ingredients: Decoupled Horizon Forecasting (DHF), which separates prediction tokens from the causally encoded context, so that longer horizons are trained without masking context and each observed value is both a forecast target and context for later forecasts; a covariate framework that natively supports known-future covariates within a causal architecture; and a two-stage pipeline that pretrains exclusively on a diverse, large-scale synthetic corpus before post-training on a mix of real and synthetic data with extended context. This report describes the model design and its benchmark results. Weights for all four models are available on Hugging Face and inference code on GitHub.

title: Rocky Linux Creator Built a New "Not Linux" Kernel in 11 Days Using AI
story_key: story|title:rocky linux creator built a new not linux kernel in 11 days using ai
content_excerpt: Gregory Kurtzer is no stranger to the Linux world. He created CentOS, and when Red Hat messed it up , he started Rocky Linux as the community replacement. He also co-founded CIQ, the company offering enterprise support around Rocky. His latest project has nothing to do with rebuilding another Linux distro, though. He has built an entirely new operating system kernel, and he didn't write most of the code himself. An AI agent did. The project is called Ginux . It's an independent, Rust-first x86-64 kernel. Which simply means it is NOT a fork of the Linux kernel. It has its own memory management, scheduler, process model, filesystems, networking, and device support, all written from scratch. The most interesting part is that even though it is not Linux, it is Linux-compatible. Ginux implements the Linux ABI (the binary interface compiled programs use to talk to the kernel), so existing Linux binaries can run on it unmodified. In the project's own terms, Linux is a "personality" that Ginux exposes, not the kernel running underneath. Now, the name Ginux may sound like a mix of GNU and Linux. I hate to disappoint you, it is not the case here. The G in Ginux stands for GPT. Greg. Kurtzer jokes in the README that, to keep his ego within limits, the G officially stands for GPT. Why GPT? Because it was coded entirely by (Chat) GPT 5.6 Sol. In 11 days, I built a new Linux-compatible operating system kernel that boots Rocky Linux 10 with systemd, all using Human-Directed Agentic Engineering (HDAE). I call it Ginux. It is an independent, Rust-first x86-64 kernel (not a Linux fork) with its own memory management, boot… Ginux builds as a single GINUX.EFI image that boots straight through UEFI, with no Linux host kernel involved. It runs isolated "domains", each with its own processes, address space, filesystem, and lifecycle. The project describes these as stronger boundaries than OCI containers or Linux namespaces. It can also pull and verify OCI container images and use them to assemble a domain's root filesystem. That's how it gets Rocky Linux 10 booted all the way to systemd's multi-user.target . Selected Alpine Linux programs (like the musl and BusyBox ) run too. Don't get too excited, though. Right now, Ginux runs only in a QEMU virtual machine, with no physical hardware profile, no GPU or NVMe support, and no independent security audit. title: AetherGrid, an open-source distributed AI workload orchestrator
story_key: story|title:aethergrid an open source distributed ai workload orchestrator
content_excerpt: A decentralized compute orchestration platform powered by strict Domain-Driven Design (DDD). Decoupled domain core, event-driven state reconciliation, and zero-overhead cluster management. A distributed AI workload orchestrator built around the problems that make scheduling hard at scale: exclusive execution ownership under failure, reconciliation after partial failures, and enforced resource limits. Not a CRUD tutorial with a scheduler theme. AetherGrid takes workloads, matches them against available compute nodes based on resource requirements and constraints, and manages the full lifecycle: queued, scheduled, running, completed, failed, retried, cancelled. Jobs run through workers registered against nodes, and job execution ownership is enforced through time-bound leases rather than a simple assignment flag. Every route requires API key authentication, including the endpoint that issues keys. Try it live : the full console is deployed and reachable at with real Postgres, real auth, and real API-key-gated endpoints. Most scheduler side-projects are a single main.py script wrapped in a while True loop polling an in-memory dictionary. They work fine, right up until you need to swap the persistence engine, add a new constraint type, or figure out why a job silently disappeared, or why two workers picked up the same job at once. AetherGrid was built around one rule: the domain logic doesn't know or care where the data lives. Jobs, nodes, workers, and the allocation algorithm are pure Python with zero infrastructure dependencies. The database is a detail, not the foundation. This project is a concrete demonstration that these architectural patterns aren't just conference-talk vocabulary; they're guardrails that keep a codebase understandable as it grows, and as its correctness requirements get harder. Every non-obvious decision in this codebase, why a domain rule lives where it does, why an obvious-looking shortcut was rejected, what broke and how it got fixed, is written down at the moment it was made, not reconstructed afterward for a portfolio. The ADRs live in . A few worth reading directly if you want to see the reasoning, not just the conclusion: If you're evaluating whether someone can operate at a systems level rather than a feature level, this is the fastest way to check. Domain : Job , Node , Worker , Lease , Event , and ApiKey aggregates enforce their own invariants. The scheduling algorithm and job lifecycle state machine live here as plain Python

title: Clearing the FoG: Training KG Agents to Retrieve the Evidence Behind Their Answers
summary: Large language models (LLMs) can answer many factual questions correctly, but a correct answer is not necessarily a supported one. For an LLM agent, a knowledge graph (KG) plays two roles: as a source of answers, it supplies facts that the model lacks; as a source of evidence, it supplies the supporting triples that make an answer traceable and auditable. However, existing KG agents treat the KG only as a source of answers: their training data carries answers but not evidence, and their training rewards check the answer but not the retrieved evidence, so agents often answer correctly without retrieving the supporting triples. We propose FoG, a framework that trains KG agents to retrieve the evidence behind their answers. FoG consists of evidence-grounded synthesis, a KG interaction agent, and an evidence-coverage process reward (ECPR): the synthesis recursively hides explicit entities behind verifiable sub-questions, so that every question carries its supporting triples by construction; the agent records the triples returned by the KG; and ECPR credits each supporting triple to the turn that first retrieves it. Experiments on three KGQA benchmarks demonstrate that FoG enables 3B--4B open-source agents to outperform substantially larger baselines in answer accuracy and evidence coverage, with zero-shot cross-KG transfer.

title: GTFormer: A Syntax-Free Graph Network Alternative to Transformers for 8192$\times$ Length Extrapolation in Linear Time
summary: Self-attention mechanisms have established the Transformer as the dominant backbone across natural language processing, source code intelligence, and automated theorem proving. However, all-to-all pairwise token comparison enforces a quadratic $\mathcal{O}(N^2)$ compute and memory barrier alongside severe softmax attention dilution as sequence length $N$ scales beyond the training horizon. Inspired by recent advances in algebraic graph learning (\textbf{WPNet}), this work introduces \textbf{GTFormer}, a syntax-free hierarchical Graph Neural Network (GNN) that replaces flat self-attention for general long-context sequence modeling. GTFormer organizes raw token streams into a bounded-degree hierarchy combining a balanced binary reduction tree ($\lceil \log_2 N \rceil$ depth), horizontal boundary-bridging shift edges, random expander shortcuts, multi-channel convex highway gating, and a top-down broadcast pass. Across eight long-context code, log, and multi-hop retrieval benchmarks trained exclusively on sequences of length $N \le 512$, GTFormer extrapolates zero-shot to $N = 4{,}194{,}304$ ($8192\times$) on a single commodity GPU in linear $\mathcal{O}(N)$ memory, maintaining near-perfect accuracy where standard and RoPE Transformers suffer from out-of-distribution attention collapse and out-of-memory exhaustion.

content_excerpt: We've built internal agents at LangChain across marketing, sales, and engineering, and they have completely changed how those teams work. They weren't easy to get right. We spent a lot of time solving the problems that come with a multiplayer harness, and every team landed on the same core primitives: To ground this discussion, a brief overview of the three main agents we have at LangChain: GTM Agent : a proactive, always-on agent that assists with GTM activities. Monitors and responds to emails, to new qualified leads, sends daily briefs, can answer questions about accounts, can run outbound motions OpenSWE : our engineering agent, can work on and draft PRs, but also runs code review over all PRs Content Studio : our marketing agent, can draft assets (blogs, images, PowerPoints, videos) in our style and with knowledge of our positioning All of these agents are built in the same way. We think this is a general recipe for building company harnesses. All our agents live where people already work, which for us is Slack. They each have their own Slack apps , and can be DM’d or tagged in a channel. One benefit of working with these agents in channels is that others can see how people use it. One nice thing we added was the concept of “breaking” out a conversation in Slack. Oftentimes, a great conversation would be happening and you’d want to add in your agent to get their opinion or get them to do something. But if they ran in that thread it would pollute the human conversation and distract. So we added an easy way for agents to “breakout” into their own thread in the channel. There are some user experiences that are best NOT done in Slack. For example, when reviewing emails GTM Agent wants me to send, it's fine to do that in a one-off way in Slack, but if there is a big backlog it's not a fun experience at all to track those from Slack messages. title: vLLM Delivers Day-0 Support for MiniMax-M3.1-Flash
summary: Day-0 vLLM support for MiniMax-M3.1-Flash on NVIDIA Blackwell, NVIDIA Rubin, and AMD MI350-series GPUs, with NVFP4 MSA kernels, NVFP4 MegaMoE, DSpark speculative decoding, AgentX results, and day-0 RL.

content_excerpt: MiniMax-M3.1-Flash is the latest model in the MiniMax-M3 family, with improvements across reasoning, coding, agentic, and visual tasks. It is also built for inference efficiency, with a native NVFP4 KV cache, NVFP4-quantized MoE weights, and a DSpark draft model for speculative decoding. vLLM supports MiniMax-M3.1-Flash on day 0 on NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs, on NVIDIA Rubin GPUs with dedicated Rubin kernels, and on AMD MI350-series GPUs, with strong performance on agentic workloads. Note that the model will only be available in the nightly PyPI wheel after the code is reviewed and merged upstream, which usually takes about a week. Full recipes are at vLLM Recipes , and the checkpoint is at MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-M3.1-Flash . The MiniMax-M3 model family replaces full attention with a variant of block-sparse attention ( arXiv 2606.13392 ) to make inference more efficient. The KV cache is split into blocks of 128 tokens. A lightweight indexer scores every key in the context with one index query per GQA group against a single shared index-key head, then max-pools those scores into one score per block. Main attention then runs exactly, but only over the top 16 blocks, and the most recent block is always kept. That caps each query at 2,048 keys, however long the context is. The payoff is largest in decode, which is limited by memory bandwidth. Each step still scans the index keys for the whole context, but that is only 128 bytes per token per layer, an eighth of the 1,024 bytes of K/V that dense attention would read (FP8, 4 KV heads × 128 dims). The full K/V is then read for just the 2,048 selected tokens. At long-context decode, per-step HBM traffic drops to about 12.5% of what dense attention reads. Figure 1: MiniMax Sparse Attention. Each GQA group's indexer picks its top KV blocks, and every query head in that group attends exactly over only those blocks. Step through it. MiniMax-M3.1 greatly improves inference efficiency over the previous generation: it was natively quantization-aware trained for an NVFP4 KV cache, and its routed MoE weights are stored in NVFP4. The NVFP4 experts shrink the checkpoint from 451.5 GB (MiniMax-M3-MXFP8) to 250.1 GB, which is 44.6% smaller. The NVFP4 KV cache needs 34,560 bytes per token instead of 61,440 bytes in FP8, a saving of 43.75% per token. title: Cross-request KV cache exposure in the GLM-5.3 Workers AI model, and our remediation with SGLang
summary: A configuration mismatch in GLM 5.3 on Workers AI triggered an SGLang bug that exposed KV cache pages across requests. Here is how we addressed the issue.

content_excerpt: On September 8, 2026, we were alerted by a security researcher, Gadi Evron from Knostic , to a tenant isolation issue affecting the GLM-5.3 Workers AI model ( @cf/zai-org/glm-5.3 ) starting on August 27, 2026. We have remediated the issue, and we restored the model on September 9. We have confirmed that no other model hosted on Workers AI was affected. Between August 27 and September 9, a small number of customers using the GLM 5.3 Workers AI model received responses that contained data from other customers' requests made to the same model shortly before theirs. In total, 155 responses were affected, all to prompts longer than 681,280 tokens. After excluding our own testing and the researcher's, the requests we identified are consistent in timing and volume with ordinary long-context use, not with someone repeatedly exploiting the bug. We found no evidence of deliberate exploitation. Today we are publishing this report alongside a post from SGLang, the open-source inference engine that we use, as a coordinated disclosure. This post describes the bug that caused this issue, our response timeline, and the subsequent hardening we have conducted on our production SGLang deployments. We also detail our continued efforts with the upstream maintainers of SGLang to address this and similar bugs. GLM is a text generation model from Z.ai that is built for agentic coding workflows; it is one of the many models available through Workers AI. Gadi Evron submitted a report on September 8 through our HackerOne program stating that very long prompts sent to @cf/zai-org/glm-5.3 on Workers AI sometimes returned text that belonged to other users' sessions. Cloudflare reproduced the issue the next morning and took the model offline within 40 minutes of declaring an incident. We then deployed a corrected configuration and a patched inference engine, and restored service the same day. This specific report of cross-request KV cache exposure was the result of two overlapping issues. The first was a misconfiguration of the open-source inference engine, SGLang, used by Cloudflare. We deployed GLM 5.3 with a 1,048,576-token context window, but the KV cache pool on our prefill GPUs only had room for 681,280 tokens. We were aware of this mismatch before launch. summary:
v0.32.0

Highlights

This release features 814 commits from 363 contributors (121 new)!

  • Structured decisions and generic parsers: the new POST /v1/systemone endpoint answers choice, noul and score questions over a structured state (#59299), is served by default (#60677, #60696), and also runs on Cloudflare/clef-omni (#61064), LiquidAI/d1-3B (#60676) and DiffusionGemma (#60466). The new hf tool and reasoning parser (--tool-call-parser hf, --reasoning-parser hf) reads the checkpoint's response_template, so models that ship it need no model-specific parser (#58604, #58602), in both the Python and Rust frontends (#59005).
  • Low-precision KV cache everywhere: NVFP4 KV cache now runs on SM8x and SM12x (#46963), SM90 (#60620) and with XQA decode on SM12x (#60452), and on MiniMax-M3 sparse attention on SM100 (#59300); GLM-5.x defaults to an FP8 KV cache on SM100, halving KV memory per rank with 2.3-5.5% more throughput at a 7-11% TTFT cost in the PR's benchmark (#60140, #60281); fp8_ds_mla on SM90 gives GLM-5.3-Flash up to 31% more output throughput (#59246); ROCm gains the 4-bit ultraquant_4bit KV cache with about 2x the density of FP8 (#57057).
  • Model Runner V2: a GPU n-gram speculator with variable-length drafts (#40704), Elastic EP (#53934), pipeline parallelism with prefill context parallelism for MLA models (#59139), a stock torch.compile mode (#59079), and MRV2 is now the default on ROCm with the model-specific MRV1 exceptions removed (#56360).
  • Faster startup and serving: vllm download-kernels installs FlashInfer's precompiled kernels (#58765); vllm preload --preload-autotune keeps the FlashInfer autotune table warm across restarts (#60085); a shared-memory tensor arena broadcasts large multimodal tensors to workers with one copy (#51207); tokenizers and processors load from the local snapshot (#60825); and with --api-server-count above 1 each connection goes to the least-loaded API worker, for 43-85% more req/s on short requests (Qwen3-0.6B, 32 input / 1 output tokens) in the PR's benchmark (#60723).
  • Model support: new EmbeddingGemma 2 omni-modal embeddings (#60254), MiniCPM-V 4.7 (#58674) and Nemotron 3.5 ASR (#59827); video input in the Transformers modeling backend (#57441); GLM-5.3 sparse MLA index conversions reused across layers (3.5-3.9x on that kernel, #59464) and fused multi-step draft decode (13.3% at concurrency 1, #57443); HiSparse per-request residency caching for up to 58% more throughput on GLM-5.3-NVFP4 on B200 with long, fully GPU-resident contexts at high concurrency (#60083).
  • Security: fixes for GHSA-4hhp-h66f-j5j7 (chat template resource exhaustion, #50300), GHSA-q97c-p368-75c4 (tokenizer max_token_id, #59491) and GHSA-frvg-qw88-hww9 (P2P ZMQ socket exhaustion, #51504); CORS no longer allows every origin by default (#61009); untrusted images are limited to raster formats (#60022); shared-memory multimodal cache handles are signed (#59357); and JSON schemas nested deeper than 64 levels are rejected (#60036).
  • Breaking changes: Python 3.10 dropped (#60402); default CORS origins restricted (#61009); transformers>=5.16.1,<5.20.0 and tokenizers>=0.23.2 (#57387, #59796); torch.compile sequence parallelism and AsyncTP passes removed (#60517); cascade attention removed (#61126); mamba_cache_mode="all" removed (#58997); max_tokens no longer reserved from the context window (#57035); Responses API reasoning stream events renamed (#59652).

Large Scale Serving

  • MoE communication: FlashInfer CuteDSL MegaMoE for more models via --moe-backend flashinfer_cutedsl (#54049), FP8 combine for the FlashInfer one-sided all2all (+4% at DEP8, #57995), NCCL symmetric-memory MoE reduce-scatter (9.6-16% lower latency, #49194), DeepEPv2 hybrid NVLink+RDMA mode on by default (#57991), Kimi-K3 shared experts with DeepEP v2 (#56875), and opt-in EPLB migration batching (#52641).
  • Context parallelism: decode requests sharded across PCP ranks (#52162) and TokenSpeed MLA with block-interleaved DCP for heterogeneous NIXL disaggregation (#59462).
  • KV connectors: NIXL host-buffer copies coalesced (#54483), mixed block sizes (#58860), peer metadata recovery (#55471) and Qwen3.8-Flash-Next MTP acceptance in P/D (#59997); Mooncake coalesced hybrid/MLA RDMA regions (#57952) and bootstrap retries (#55923); MoRIIO Kimi-K3 DSpark READ (#57700); DeepSeek-V4.1 P/D skipping bounded replay for loaded KV (#59197); and KVCR pool-and-index API (#59899).
  • Data parallelism: streaming requests pinned to their engine (#59017), per-engine RNG streams (#59788), and placement groups without ray[default] (#57648).

Hardware & Performance

  • NVIDIA: native 64-head FlashMLA sparse prefill on SM100 (1.16-1.18x TTFT, #60029), block-FP8 DeepGEMM experts skipping padding (#59128), SM120 split-K attention (#58482), DGX Spark Qwen4Exp GEMM plans (#59753, #59632, #60027), OAI Triton MXFP4 MoE on SM12x (#58877), and FlashInfer autotune cache per rank (#57635).
  • AMD ROCm: DeepSeek-V4 AITER MegaMoEV2 via --moe-backend aiter_mega_moe (#59685) with opt-in shared-expert fusion (3-8%, #61004), opt-in mono decode for DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash on MI355X (VLLM_ROCM_MONO_DECODE=1, #60397), opt-in Gluon sparse MLA (up to +16% on GLM-5.2, #53492), paged MXFP4 indexer (#58671), opt-in a4w4 MoE for DSv4 (#58819), ultraquant_4bit KV cache (#57057), aiter_flydsl GDN prefill (#57560), Kimi-K3 prefill checkpoints (about 20% better TTFT, #58344), fused MLA decode (#57640) and per-rank latent MoE shards (#59591), GLM-5.3-Flash split-K sparse MLA decode (5-15% lower ITL, #58584), native merge_attn_states (2.4x, #60159), ROCM_SEGMENTED_ATTN for RDNA (#59132), gfx11 W4A16 tuning (up to 23% TTFT, #56301), MRV2 default with model-specific MRV1 exceptions removed (#56360), and fixes for sleep-mode segfaults on ROCm 7.2+ (#60367) and MLA weight reloads (#60389).
  • Intel XPU: MLA in FLASH_ATTN_MLA (#58297), Arc Pro B70 FP8 GEMM (2.0-2.73x, #56063) and fused MoE configs (#53065), fused SYCL LayerNorm (#57172), and fixes for Gemma-2 softcap (#58936) and DP+EP MoE (#57787).
  • CPU: vectorized sampler (up to 58x on s390x, #53913), aarch64 causal conv1d (about 9%, #54093), POWER10 AWQ/GPTQ (#59149), and PowerPC dtype=auto choosing bfloat16 (#58528).
  • Other: tpu-inference v0.31.0 (#60190) and out-of-tree platforms registering multiple attention backends (#41091).

Quantization

  • New capabilities: online re-quantization of linear layers (--quantization-config.linear fp8_per_channel, #55684), per-token NVFP4 CuTe-DSL MoE (#50030) with ReLU2 (#56740), MXFP4 MoE oracle with CUTLASS W4A4 and BF16 fallback (#60079), compressed-tensors MXFP4 MoE with FP8 activations (#59815), ModelOpt IQ2_XS/IQ2_XXS/Q8_0 on SM120/SM121 (#59604), int4_per_token_head KV with non-power-of-two heads (#56198), and Humming preferred over Marlin on SM90 (#56997).
  • Fixes: silent CUTLASS NVFP4/MXFP4 MoE corruption under EP (#59042), GPTQ with non-default safetensors names (#60411), moe_wna16 8-bit asymmetric zero points (#58950), and ModelOpt mixed-precision NVFP4 detection (#56050).

API & Frontend

  • New endpoints and options: /v1/systemone (#59299, #60677, #60696), hf parser (#58604), vllm download-kernels (#58765), output_mode: "text" and stop_reason in /inference/v1/generate (#58588, #60251), mm_payload for render requests (#61427, #60728), Responses min_p and stop_token_ids (#48084, #56592), LLM.chat(priority=...) (#57243), and /generative_scoring cache_salt (#60841).
  • Behavior: max_tokens is an upper bound instead of a reservation, so long prompts are no longer rejected (#57035); least-loaded API worker selection (#60723); tool parser compatibility checked at startup (#59749).
  • Tool calling and structured output: parallel_tool_calls=false enforced (#50502, #59298), tool_choice="required" streaming (#60354) and native XML parsers (#47512), Step-3.5 and minimax_m3 on the parser engine (#59321, #59743), xgrammar propertyNames (#57594), and LoRA PEFT rank_pattern/alpha_pattern applied with unsupported features rejected (#59801, #60225).
  • Rust frontend: --grpc-port (#59659), --stream-interval (#60589), logprob_token_ids (#59549), Control.Shutdown with vllm-proto 0.5.0 (#59316), qwen3_json parser (#60136), and Kimi K3 grammar fixes (#59190, #59395).

Security

  • GHSA-4hhp-h66f-j5j7: chat templates are validated statically and rendered under a timeout (VLLM_CHAT_TEMPLATE_RENDER_TIMEOUT), user-supplied chat_template in Responses chat_template_kwargs is rejected, and the Rust frontend caps template execution (#50300).
  • GHSA-q97c-p368-75c4: tokenizer max_token_id off-by-one fixed (#59491).
  • GHSA-frvg-qw88-hww9: P2P ZMQ peer sessions are bounded by VLLM_P2P_MAX_PEERS (default 128), VLLM_P2P_HANDSHAKE_TIMEOUT_S (default 30) and VLLM_P2P_IDLE_TIMEOUT_S (default 300), so unique peer addresses can no longer exhaust ZMQ sockets (#51504).
  • Default CORS settings no longer allow every origin in the Python and Rust frontends; set --allowed-origins to permit browser origins (#61009).
  • Untrusted images are opened with a raster-format allowlist (ALLOWED_IMAGE_FORMATS), denying EPS/PostScript and WMF (#60022); shared-memory multimodal cache handles are HMAC-signed and forged handles rejected (#59357).
  • Structured-output JSON schemas nested more than 64 levels return 400 (#60036); chunked /v1/embeddings requests keep cache_salt (#47696); Phi-4 MM audio no longer holds multi-GiB attention matrices (#60614); DeepSeek-OCR zero-sum pixel tensors no longer kill EngineCore (#59417).
  • Security dependency bumps: aiohttp>=3.14.3, pillow>=12.3.0, cryptography, urllib3, pyjwt and others (#59249, #59315, #59427).

Dependencies

  • transformers>=5.16.1,<5.20.0 (minimum raised from 5.10.4, #57387, #59762) and tokenizers>=0.23.2 (#59796).
  • NIXL 1.5.0 (#56907), CuTe DSL 4.8.0 block-scale APIs (#59480), humming-kernels==0.1.17 with initial Rubin support (#61556, #61858), InstantTensor 0.2.2 (#61167), and flashinfer-jit-cache excluded from wheel install_requires (#60052).
  • ROCm: AITER 0.1.24.post1 (#59794) and MoRI v1.2.3.post1 (#56073). XPU: auto-round-lib 0.16.0 (#60976). TPU: tpu-inference v0.31.0 (#60190).

Build

  • Python 3.11-3.14 supported (#60402); macOS wheels built with the stable ABI (#60312); CUDA source builds require GCC 13 and fail early otherwise (#60259); Docker images compile Python bytecode at build time for faster container startup (#55422); VLLM_USE_PRECOMPILED finds a compatible published wheel within the last 20 commits (#58871); the vendored DeepGEMM uses TORCH_LIBRARY (abi3, #48962).

Breaking Changes & Deprecations

  • Python 3.10 is no longer supported; the minimum is Python 3.11 (#60402).
  • Default CORS origins changed from * to none; set --allowed-origins for browser clients (#61009).
  • transformers>=5.16.1,<5.20.0 and tokenizers>=0.23.2 are required (#57387, #59796).
  • The torch.compile sequence parallelism and AsyncTP passes were removed, along with PassConfig.enable_sp, fuse_gemm_comms and sp_min_token_num; model-level sequence parallelism is unaffected (#60517).
  • Cascade attention was removed; --disable-cascade-attn still parses but only warns and will be removed in v0.33.0 (#61126).
  • mamba_cache_mode="all" was removed; --mamba-cache-mode all now fails validation (#58997).
  • Previously deprecated APIs were removed: wait_for_inflight_requests (use mode="wait"), AsyncLLM.pause_generation(), IOProcessor.output_to_response, vllm.scripts.main() and vllm bench throughput --dataset (#60923). The sonnet benchmark dataset was removed as scheduled (#60129). Tensorizer support was removed from LoRA (#60024), and the PyO3 vllm._rust_tool_parser bridge was removed (#59744).
  • API changes: max_tokens is treated as an upper bound on output rather than reserved from the context window (#57035); Responses API streaming uses response.content_part.added/done with part.type="reasoning_text" instead of response.reasoning_part.added/done (#59652); SamplingParams.prompt_logprob_token_ids is per row (#56984); /inference/v1/generate logprobs use integer token IDs (#58181); sleep API responses are standardized and invalid levels return 400 (#52864); return_mm_kwargs is deprecated in favor of mm_payload (#61427).
  • Watermarking: when the engine has watermarking configured, an omitted request field means enabled and only false opts out; unsupported combinations warn and fall back (#56801).
  • Rust frontend: qwen3_xml now parses Qwen3-Coder XML (alias of qwen3_coder); use the new qwen3_json for the JSON format (#60136).
  • New defaults: shared-memory tensor arena on (#51207); GLM-5.x FP8 KV cache on SM100 with --kv-cache-dtype auto (#60140, #60281); VLLM_DEEPEP_V2_ALLOW_HYBRID_MODE=1 (#57991); Humming preferred over Marlin on SM90 (#56997); sparse_mla_prefill_workspace_factor 2 above 256K max_model_len (#61023); MRV2 on ROCm with model-specific MRV1 exceptions removed (#56360); VLLM_ROCM_AITER_MLA_DCP_VERIFY=auto (#59965); dtype=auto picks bfloat16 on PowerPC (#58528); MXFP4 W4A4 checkpoints fall back to W4A16 with a warning when no W4A4 kernel exists (#60079).
  • Stricter validation: incompatible --prefix-match-unit (#58021), max_num_scheduled_tokens=0 (#60714), HiSparse with cudagraph_mode=FULL (#59688), and negative --device-ids (#49053) are rejected at startup.
